fields.Front: State the two halves of the Week 2 definition of encapsulation.
fields.Back: (1) Bundling the data (attributes) and the methods that operate on that data into a single unit, the class. (2) Restricting access to some of the object's components, so the internal state is protected from direct access and from modification by other objects.

fields.Front: Why does encapsulation promote getters and setters instead of direct data access?
fields.Back: A setter is a place to put additional validation or logic BEFORE a change is made, and a getter is a place to compute or format a value on the way out. The public interface stays the same while the implementation is free to change.

fields.Front: In the Person example, what do getName() and setName() do, and what is the argument for the setter?
fields.Back: string getName() { return name; } returns a copy of the private name; void setName(string newName) { name = newName; } is the only way to change it. Today it simply assigns; tomorrow it could reject empty strings or trim whitespace without touching a single caller.

fields.Front: What small improvement would you make to string getName() in the Person example?
fields.Back: Declare it const: string getName() const, as Week 1's Account::getBalance() was, because it only reads the object. Returning const std::string& would also avoid a copy.

fields.Front: What does the BankAccount constructor do with a negative initial balance, and why does it matter?
fields.Back: if (initial_balance >= 0) balance = initial_balance; else balance = 0; A negative initial balance is silently replaced with 0, so the object is born valid. Compare Week 1's Account, whose constructor accepted any value.

deposit adds only if (amount > 0), so zero or negative deposits are ignored. withdraw subtracts only if (amount > 0 && amount <= balance), so the balance can never go negative. Both failures are silent.

fields.Front: Why does the slides' BankAccount deliberately have no setBalance()?
fields.Back: So every change passes through deposit/withdraw, which validate; balance is read-only through getBalance(). The design principle: expose operations that make sense in the domain, not raw field access. A setBalance() would defeat the validation.

fields.Front: What would improve on the silent failures in BankAccount, and what is the slides' point anyway?
fields.Back: Returning a bool or throwing an exception would report the failure. The slide's point is that the DECISION lives in one place: because balance is private, the class alone decides what a valid change is.

fields.Text: The two key aspects of encapsulation are {{c1::data hiding}}, achieved with access modifiers, and {{c1::getter and setter methods}}, which give a place for validation.

Access modifiers: {{c1::private}} members are accessible only within the class they are declared; {{c1::protected}} members are accessible within the class and by derived classes; {{c1::public}} members are accessible from outside the class.
fields.Extra: The default design stance: attributes private, behaviour public, protected reserved for what a subclass genuinely needs.

fields.Text: The three benefits of encapsulation are {{c1::security}} (prevents unintended interference with the object's data), {{c1::maintainability}} (internal implementation can change while the public interface stays the same), and {{c1::reusability}}.
BankAccount account(1000); ... deposit(500); ... withdraw(200); prints `Initial Balance: ${{c1::1000}}, After Deposit: ${{c1::1500}}, After Withdrawal: ${{c1::1300}}`.
Encapsulation = {{c1::bundling}} data with the methods that operate on it, plus {{c1::restricting access}} so the internal state is protected from direct access and modification by other objects.
fields.Extra: Saying it is only bundling is the classic exam mistake.

fields.Text: In BankAccount, deposit requires `{{c1::amount > 0}} and withdraw requires {{c1::amount > 0 && amount <= balance}}`, so the balance can never go {{c1::negative}}.
The BankAccount constructor keeps initial_balance only when {{c1::initial_balance >= 0}}, otherwise setting balance to {{c1::0}}, so the object is {{c1::born valid}}.
